newsitem.title: LEBANON: Pope says Lebanon must regain full independence.
newsitem.headline: Pope says Lebanon must regain full independence.

text.p: Pope John Paul called on Sunday for the complete independence of Lebanon but stopped short of explicitly echoing an outright demand from the country's bishops for the withdrawal of Israeli and Syrian forces.

The Roman Catholic Pontiff made his plea in a 200-page document on Lebanon's future published at the end of a huge open air-mass on Beirut's former Green Line battlefront on the final day of his weekend visit to the country.

In the document, called an Apostolic Exhortation, the Pope issued an impassioned appeal for reconciliation among Christians and Moslems in order to build real peace following Lebanon's long and devastating civil war.
He also urged minority Christians, who emerged defeated from the 1975-1990 war and have since complained of discrimination and loss of rights, to remain in the country.
"Obviously, all this also supposes that the country recovers its total independence, complete sovereignty and unambiguous freedom," the Pope wrote.

Elsewhere in the document, he referred to the "menacing occupation of southern Lebanon" and to the "presence of non-Lebanese armed forces on the territory" as among difficulties that faced the country.
"All this feeds passions, as well as the fear that the values of democracy and civilisation which this country represents might be compromised," the Pope wrote.
Around 35,000 Syrian troops are stationed in Lebanon and 2,000 Israeli troops hold a border occupation zone in the south.
That they should pull out was implicit in the Pope's writings but he did not make the call openly nor refer directly to Syria and Israel.
The oblique approach contrasted with a blunt demand for the troops to leave made by Lebanese bishops in 1995 in their conclusions from a Vatican synod on the Church in Lebanon.

Their demand for the withdrawal of Syrian forces as well as Israeli troops and a denunciation of political imprisonment, torture, and other abuses by the state shocked Moslems, who sent an envoy to the Vatican to discuss it.
Sunday's papal document, entitled "A New Hope for Lebanon", was the 76-year-old Pope's response to the bishops' assembly and formally concluded the lengthy synod process.

Thousands of Christians left Lebanon during the civil war. Many of those who remain are critical of the pro-Syrian government, which they accuse of surrendering its powers of decision to Damascus, and complain that they are marginalised.

Cardinal Nasrallah Sfeir, patriarch of the Maronite Church, drew loud chants of "Freedom, freedom" at a service with the Pope on Saturday when he said young Lebanese seeking democracy and human rights were barred from political advancement.

The papal document picked up the same theme, though more obliquely, saying peace in Lebanon could not be more than an absence of conflict, unless all the country's denominations were able to play an equal part in its affairs.

"No spiritual community can live if it is not recognised, if it finds itself in precarious conditions and if it does not have the chance to participate fully in the life of the nation," the Pope wrote.
He said the authorities in Lebanon had to ensure that all communities enjoyed the same rights and had to put the common good above sectarian or personal interests.

"To be really itself, Lebanon needs all its sons and daughters and all components of its population. Each has its place in the country and must rediscover the taste for living there and taking up the challenge of its future," he said.

The Pope, who is on his first visit to the Middle East, has hailed Lebanon, with its patchwork of 17 officially recognised religions, as an example for a region where Christian communities are in decline.

In his document, he urged all Lebanese to "take up the arms of peace and justice" and seek reconciliation so as to heal the wounds of war. "One must never forget that a gesture of peace can disarm an adversary," the Pope wrote.

"For men of goodwill, it is unthinkable that members of the same human community, living on the same soil, come to distrust each other, to oppose each other and to exclude each other in the name of their respective religions."
